NEW RELIGIOUS MOVEMENTS, CULTS AND SECTS

INTRODUCTION
- During the twentieth century the religious landscape of the world changed dramatically.
- Religious plurality (many religions) has growing influence on society. Better travel and communication mean more exposure to, and understanding of, different beliefs.
- There has always been religious diversity, but there has been an unprecedented growth of new and alternative forms of religious belief and practice.
- This has led to a COUNTER-CULTURE that answers two things:
- 1. the personal search for spiritual freedom and self-expression;
- 2. a wish for an alternative to modernity and a return to an ideal or definitive form of a particular religion.
- George Boran: "There is a feeling [in today's world] of being tossed around, with no secure anchors to prevent shipwreck on the surrounding rocks."
- This diversity is a threat to some and a cause to celebrate for others.
- NRMs (new religious movements, commonly called cults) are often in the news. TV and newspapers report the tragic results of destructive cult leaders; films and TV sometimes show NRMs as bizarre and dangerous.
- In many Irish towns and cities, a recruiter for an NRM may ask you, "Can you spare a few moments?"
- There is a marked decline, especially among young people, in involvement in the major Christian churches, but people are still searching for MEANING, IDENTITY and PURPOSE.
- Some NRMs are influenced by Eastern thought (Hindu or Buddhist practices); some look to pre-Christian Druidism; more often they offer alternative approaches to ecological and global issues for people disillusioned with the established churches.
- NRMs offer an alternative to official institutional religion and are very diverse, so they are hard to categorise.
- They are "NEW" because they are a significant contemporary expression of the search for meaning in modern society.
- They are "RELIGIOUS" because they offer answers to the fundamental questions of life and reflect a religious vision of the world.

KEY TERMS (ONE-LINE DEFINITIONS)
- New Religious Movement (NRM): a modern religious group offering an alternative to institutional religion; the term preferred by most sociologists instead of "cult" or "sect".
- Sect: a religious group that separates from its parent religion but keeps the same world view and sources of revelation, emphasising particular aspects of it.
- Cult: any religious group that differs significantly in one or more respects of belief or practice from the normative (standard) expressions of religion in the culture.
- Authority (of the leader): in many NRMs the leader's authority is absolute and unquestioned.
- Reductionist: reducing a parent tradition to selected excerpts and presenting them simplistically.
- Fundamentalist: interpreting sacred texts or doctrine in a rigid, literal, simplistic way.
- Exclusionist: claiming that only the group's members will be saved or have the truth.
- Love bombing: unconditional acceptance and constant reassurance to make a recruit feel totally loved.
- Asceticism: a strict, self-denying lifestyle.
- Proselytising: trying to convert people from their former religion.
- Hare Krishna movement (ISKCON): the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, founded in America in 1968, with Indian roots.
- New Age movement (NAM): an umbrella term for a network of beliefs drawing on Eastern traditions, holistic health, magic, astrology and ecology.

WHAT'S IN A NAME? CULTS AND SECTS
- "Cult" and "sect" are more familiar than "NRM" but cause difficulties: they are often used interchangeably.
- People often assume all cults are bad.
- Experiences of cults range from finding self-worth, belonging and direction, to physical and mental control, loss of freedom and lack of contact with loved ones.
- All major world religions have developed offshoots over time; these are usually called SECTS.
- A sect separates from the parent religion (the chapter says "sector" means to cut) but keeps the same world view and the same sources of revelation. It emphasises particular aspects of the parent religion.

EXAMPLES OF SECTS
- Judaism: Hasidic Jews are ultra-orthodox in belief and practice.
- Judaism: the Jewish Renewal Movement in New York emphasises experience-based spirituality and Jewish identity.
- Christianity: Methodism began as a revivalist movement within the Anglican Church (which itself dates back to the Reformation).
- Buddhism: Soka Gakkai and Zen Buddhism are sects of Buddhism.

EXAMPLES OF CULTS
- The Branch Davidian Movement, led by David Koresh.
- The Children of God Movement, led by David Beg.
- The Unification Church ("Moonies"), led by Sun Myung Moon.

PHILIP BARNES ON TERMS (WORLD RELIGIONS)
- There is no simple answer to the debate on terms.
- In a clearly post-Christian society like Britain, "NRM" may be the best name for non-conventional groups.
- In Ireland, where Christianity still has social significance, "sect" and "cult" may still be meaningful.
- It is not necessary to come down firmly on one side.

SEVEN CHARACTERISTICS OF NRMS
- 1. AUTHORITY OF THE LEADER: the leader's authority is often absolute, even overriding the group's own teachings or writings. This unquestioned authority can lead members to murder and suicide. Examples: Jim Jones in Guyana; David Koresh in Waco, Texas; Luc Jouret in Switzerland; Shoko Asahara and the Aum sect in Japan.
- 2. TOTAL CONTROL OF MEMBERS: groups decide what members eat and wear, when they sleep and work, even whom they marry. Members watch others and are watched. Forbidding contact with loved ones makes members rely on the cult for emotional support. Often strong (virulent) opposition to members' former churches or faiths.
- 3. REDUCTIONIST AND FUNDAMENTALIST: they use selected excerpts of a "parent" tradition (often a major world faith) and present them in a simplistic, often fundamentalist way. This often reflects an escape or alienation from the reality of daily life.
- 4. EXCLUSIONIST: only their members will be saved, only they have the truth. Often a very negative attitude to society and no interest in wider social commitment or the struggle for justice - only their own members matter.
- 5. CRITICAL REFLECTION PREVENTED: members may read only the group's writings; everything else is "unholy". Discussion, even conversation, with non-members can be forbidden. Constant activity (work, prayer, chanting), restricted diet and constant "companionship" make independent thinking and leaving very hard. Intense proselytising imposes unconditional obedience.
- 6. MONEY: members spend much time and energy raising money, so many groups are extremely wealthy. This increases the power of the group, especially the leader.
- 7. MISSIONARY ZEAL: at airports, shopping areas, concerts and front doors, NRMs show great drive to expand membership. They can be very active, even militant, recruiting aggressively in a spirit of conquest.

WHO JOINS, AND WHY?
- People searching for meaning, identity and purpose, and answers to life's big questions, which they have not found (or not recognised) in the churches.
- Often bright, idealistic and generous people.
- Many are disaffected members of major faiths, especially mainline Christian churches, which lose members through a lack of genuine spiritual experience and fellowship.
- Three groups most likely to join:
- "IN TRANSIT": between school and university/work, adolescence and adulthood, relationships, or homes; lonely, drifting, "rootless"; often aged 18-28; searching for a different, intellectually challenging world view.
- "IN DIFFICULTY": hurt by failed romance, family rows, job loss; under pressure about career, future, marriage, goals; low self-esteem or confidence; poor sense of identity.
- "IN IGNORANCE": of their own religious tradition (scripture, history, true teaching); and of the NRM itself, except superficially, as full knowledge is often withheld from new members.

METHODS OF INFLUENCE (FR MARTIN TIERNEY, CULTS, SECTS AND NEW RELIGIOUS GROUPS)
- SIMPLE SOLUTIONS: an answer for every question and a solution to every problem. Members see themselves as a fellowship of the saved, not a mixture of saints and sinners.
- LOVE BOMBING: unconditional acceptance and constant reassurance so the recruit feels totally loved. Makes objective assessment of the group very hard.
- ASCETICISM: the strict lifestyle attracts idealistic recruits as a challenging alternative to a "take it or leave it" approach.
- CONSTANT ACTIVITY: always work, study or prayer, so little time to reflect, and members are too physically and mentally drained to reflect anyway.

HOW NRMS SUCCEED IN ATTRACTING MEMBERS
- People join for personal, social and spiritual reasons.
- PUBLICATIONS AND COMMUNICATIONS: free or cheap books widely distributed; media used to broadcast witness and testimony; backed up by personal contact - home visits and street missionary work.
- CLEAR PLANNING AND STRATEGY: careful schedules for maximum proselytising success. Invitations like "Come to our group" or "Renew your life"; reactions are recorded; second and third visits lead to a first visit to a group gathering. Welcome and respect lead to a "dual existence" (in and out of the group); then proselytising focuses on rejecting all previous religious commitment, leading to complete conversion.
- VISION AND PARTICIPATION: a new vision and hope in a world of constant activity, conflicting ideologies and pressure. Chances to take part in ministry give self-worth and identity, often lacking in large established churches; this lessens the sense of anonymity. Belonging and commitment are central.
- TEACHING, SPIRITUALITY AND MORALITY: preaching is the basic method, with simple, repetitive challenges and answers. Members listen and repeat; spiritual and moral questions are answered inside the group, without reference to the wider world. Intimacy, warmth and community reinforce the belief that the leaders' answers are absolutely correct.

THE HARE KRISHNA MOVEMENT (HIGHER LEVEL)
- Also called the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON).
- Founded in America in 1968, but with Indian roots.
- Founder: Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, a successful Indian pharmacist.
- From 1944 he expressed his religious ideas in a magazine called "Back to the Godhead".
- The response was so positive that at fifty-eight he left his wife and five children and became a Hindu monk.
- 1965: he went to America, where his Western-style Hindu philosophy aroused huge interest.
- ISKCON is now a worldwide organisation of spiritual centres, temples, farm communities, schools and institutions.
- Prabhupada receives as much respect and honour as Krishna, because he was God's "via media" (representative) who distributed God's love.
- Scripture: mainly the Bhagavad Gita ("Song of the Lord"), part of the long Hindu epic, the Mahabharata.
- It tells the story of Krishna, the eighth incarnation of the god Vishnu, and his teaching that knowledge, work and devotion are all paths to salvation.

HARE KRISHNA: SALVATION AND CHANTING (FR MARTIN TIERNEY, THE NEW ELECT)
- Salvation = a personal relationship with Krishna. "Krishna" means god.
- Chanting the Hare Krishna mantra revives Krishna consciousness; Krishna is awakened by chanting.
- The mantra: "Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna, Krishna, Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare, Hare."
- "Hare" means "O energy of the Lord"; "Krishna" means "O Lord Krishna".
- Aim: "original god-consciousness" through a strict routine of spiritual exercises and an organised lifestyle.
- Members believe the movement is the true path to salvation.

HARE KRISHNA: OTHER KEY BELIEFS
- Krishna is the highest Hindu god, the Lord, the Absolute Truth, with many incarnations.
- Jesus was not God; he was a pure devotee of Krishna, visiting from another planet.
- Hindu scriptures are authoritative. The Bible and Qur'an are genuine scriptures but have been distorted in translation and interpretation.
- After death the soul is reincarnated. How you live now decides your form in the next life.
- Death is a transition, not an end. The goal is freedom from repetitive reincarnation (the textbook words it as "to reach samsara or freedom from repetitive reincarnation").

NINE ACTS OF DEVOTIONAL SERVICE (DAILY)
- 1 Hearing about Krishna. 2 Chanting Krishna's names. 3 Reading and mixing with fellow devotees. 4 Praying to Krishna. 5 Serving Krishna in the temple. 6 Preparing food as an offering. 7 Encouraging others to come to know Krishna. 8 Encouraging others to chant Krishna's names. 9 Developing a personal relationship with Krishna.
- Regular temple ceremonies matter, and statues of Krishna are revered as in Hinduism.

LIFESTYLE OF KRISHNA FOLLOWERS
- Easily recognised: shaven heads, saffron robes, street processions.
- They sell literature, candles and incense, run vegetarian restaurants and ask for donations.
- Strict vegetarians; no fish or eggs; no tea, coffee or alcohol; no smoking.
- Gambling and frivolous sports are unworthy.
- Cleanliness is important; members shower often.
- No sex outside marriage; married couples may have sex only to have children.
- Followers live in temples and submit completely to the leader, who arranges marriages and is the final authority on scripture and ceremonies.

A TYPICAL DAY
- 3.00 get up and shower; 3.00-4.00 individual chanting; 4.00-4.30 service; 4.30-5.00 chanting; 6.00-7.00 study of the Bhagavad Gita; 7.00 breakfast; 8.00-10.00 temple chores; 10.00-18.00 on the streets raising money (short lunch at temple); 18.00 meal; 18.30-20.00 study; 20.00 hot meal; 20.30-22.00 study once chores are done.

JOINING AND CONCERNS
- New members spend the first six months in the temple learning the philosophy.
- When the temple president thinks they are ready, an elaborate initiation ceremony of FIRE is held.
- Six months later a second ceremony confirms them as full members.
- The austere routine of prayer, study and work can limit chances to reflect critically or express doubts, e.g. about the temple president's authority.
- Close relationships with non-member family and friends can be hard, especially as recruits feel totally loved and accepted.

HARE KRISHNA TODAY
- Change and sometimes decline over the last thirty years.
- The monastic lifestyle has adapted to jobs and family responsibilities; members are more involved in the everyday world.
- Three main Irish temples: Dublin, Belfast and County Fermanagh - small but committed communities; temple rooms decorated with pictures of Lord Krishna.
- Daily devotions, street witnessing and community living remain central.
- The movement has matured: more study-oriented; temples are teaching centres for devotional Hinduism; more accepted by the Asian community; festivals attract thousands of Asian Hindus.

THE NEW AGE MOVEMENT (HIGHER LEVEL)
- Hard to define: an umbrella term covering Eastern traditions, holistic health, magic, astrology and ecology.
- Central belief: a New Age of peace and enlightenment is emerging - the AGE OF AQUARIUS. We have left the astrological Age of PISCES (which has failed).
- People are to create their own salvation, not be saved by a Redeemer.
- Time to develop mystical awareness and improve the world, using horoscopes, yoga, tarot cards, fortune-telling and rebirthing.
- Religious words have very different meanings from Christianity (which NAM sees as obsolete):
- Christ = "the collective conscience of the universe"; the coming of the "Cosmic Christ" is awaited.
- Lucifer = source of all wisdom and knowledge, because he caused the fall, in which humanity's eyes were opened.
- Group meetings are called "prayer meetings". This is the age of the "spirit", of new mysticism.
- Tendency to divinise humanity, e.g. actress Shirley MacLaine: "I am God".

PHILIP BARNES ON THE NEW AGE
- No single founder and no official creed.
- Spokespersons: actress Shirley MacLaine; physicist Fritjof Capra; Sir George Trevelyan (founder of the Wrekin Trust); North American theologian Matthew Fox.
- Earlier inspirations: Helena Blavatsky (1831-91) and Alice Bailey (1880-1949).
- Best thought of as a NETWORK of interconnected groups, organisations and individuals with overlapping goals.
- Most practices are not new; they draw on contemplative traditions, especially Hinduism and Buddhism.
- Typical practices: astral projection; automatic writing; astrology and horoscopes; channelling and Spirit guides; colour therapy; divination (I Ching, Tarot); dream analysis; chanting and yoga; alternative medicine (crystals, acupuncture).
- A small number promote openly pagan (reviving pre-Christian practices) and occult practices such as black magic.
- Common emphases: dissatisfaction with materialism and secularism; dissatisfaction with conventional religion; a holistic approach to life and health; a vision of a new world order; belief that each person can change themselves and the world.
- Assignment quote: New Age "is not a religion, but is nonetheless religious"; not a philosophy or a science, but "an amorphous amalgam of the esoteric and the occult, of myths and magic ... with a touch of Christianity and a few ideas derived from astrophysics".

CARDINAL GODFRIED DANNEELS, "CHRIST OR AQUARIUS": FOUR CORNERSTONES
- 1. A SCIENTIFIC BASE: humankind woven into the universal fabric of life, with no distinction between soul and body, God and the world, heaven and earth.
- 2. ORIENTAL RELIGIONS: Eastern thought on unity, fusion and the cycle of rebirth.
- 3. A NEW PSYCHOLOGY: birth and death experiences and the "collective unconscious" said to be in all people.
- 4. ASTROLOGY: esoteric, secret knowledge of horoscopes; the era of Aquarius and new world order beginning in 2000 CE promising cosmic love and happiness.
- Christian response (Danneels): the value of prayer and the importance of the "I-Thou" relationship between God and God's people.

THE NEW AGE TODAY
- The "new spiritual age" of Aquarius has arrived, but its promise of universal community and world fraternity is not materialising.
- Many say the movement is in decline; followers may move to other spiritual searches.
- Some practices will remain a source of relaxation and transformation, but the movement's future is "as fragmented as the ideals it embraces".

ESSAY TITLES (FROM THE ASSIGNMENTS)
- NRMs: paths where pilgrims "spend money on what cannot nourish" (Isaiah 55:2).
- It is the task of mainstream churches and faiths to face the challenge of community building and spiritual nourishment.
- The spiritual marketplace is wide open to exploitation and manipulation.

CHAPTER KEY TERMS LIST
- New Religious Movements, Cults, Sect, Authority, Reductionist, Fundamentalist, Exclusionist, Love-bombing, Asceticism, Hare Krishna movement, New Age movement.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between a cult and a sect, giving one example of each.

rows.prompt: Explain why NRMs are described as both 'new' and 'religious'.
rows.model_answer: They are 'new' because they are a significant contemporary expression of the search for meaning in modern society. They are 'religious' because they offer answers to the fundamental questions of life and reflect a religious vision of the world.

rows.prompt: Explain how the authority of the leader can be dangerous in an NRM. Give one example.
rows.model_answer: In many NRMs the leader's authority is absolute and unquestioned, even overriding the group's own teachings. This can lead members to murder and suicide. Examples include Jim Jones in Guyana and David Koresh in Waco, Texas.

rows.prompt: Explain why critical reflection is a threat to NRMs and how they prevent it.
rows.model_answer: Independent thinking might lead members to question the leader or leave. So NRMs forbid reading anything except the group's writings and ban discussion with non-members. Constant activity, restricted diet and constant 'companionship' leave no time or energy to think independently.

rows.prompt: Describe the three types of people most likely to join an NRM.

People 'in difficulty' - hurt by failed romance, family rows or job loss, or with low self-esteem. People 'in ignorance' - of their own religious tradition and of the NRM's full teaching.

rows.prompt: Explain 'love bombing' and 'constant activity' as methods of influence.

rows.prompt: Describe the lifestyle rules of Hare Krishna followers.

Sex is only within marriage for having children, and followers live in temples and obey the leader, who arranges marriages.

rows.prompt: Explain how the New Age movement uses religious terms differently from Christianity.

People create their own salvation rather than being saved by a Redeemer, and humanity is divinised, as in Shirley MacLaine's 'I am God'.

rows.prompt: Outline the main characteristics of New Religious Movements (NRMs).
rows.model_answer: Many NRMs show some or all of seven traits. First, the authority of the leader is often absolute, even overriding the group's own writings; this unquestioned authority has led members to murder and suicide, as with Jim Jones in Guyana, David Koresh in Waco, Texas, Luc Jouret in Switzerland and Shoko Asahara's Aum sect in Japan. Second, there is total control of members: what they eat and wear, when they sleep and work, even whom they marry; contact with loved ones may be forbidden so members rely on the cult. Third, they are reductionist and fundamentalist, using selected excerpts of a parent faith in a simplistic way. Fourth, they are exclusionist, claiming only their members will be saved and showing little interest in wider society or justice. Fifth, critical reflection is prevented: members read only the group's writings, may not talk to outsiders, and constant activity and restricted diet make independent thought and leaving very difficult. Sixth, money is central: members spend much time fundraising, so many groups are very wealthy and the leader's power grows. Seventh, they show missionary zeal, recruiting at airports, shopping areas, concerts and front doors, sometimes aggressively and in a spirit of conquest.

rows.prompt: Why do people join New Religious Movements, and what methods do NRMs use to attract and keep members?
rows.model_answer: People join NRMs because they are searching for meaning, identity and purpose and answers to life's big questions, which they have not found in the churches. They are often bright, idealistic and generous, and many are disaffected members of mainline churches that lack genuine spiritual experience and fellowship. Those most at risk are 'in transit' (between school and work, homes or relationships, often aged 18-28, lonely and rootless), 'in difficulty' (after failed romance, family rows or job loss, or with low self-esteem) and 'in ignorance' of their own tradition and of the NRM's real teaching. Fr Martin Tierney describes methods of influence: simple solutions to every problem; love bombing, where unconditional acceptance makes it hard to judge the group objectively; asceticism, which appeals to idealists; and constant activity, leaving no time to reflect. NRMs also use free books, media testimony, home visits and street work, with clear planning: invitations, recorded responses, repeat visits, a 'dual existence', then rejection of past religious commitment and complete conversion. They offer vision, participation in ministry and a sense of belonging that reduces anonymity, while repetitive preaching answers every question within the group, convincing members the leaders are absolutely right.
rows.marking_scheme: Reasons for joining: up to 8 marks (searching for meaning/identity/purpose; idealistic; disaffected church members; in transit, in difficulty, in ignorance). Methods: up to 12 marks (simple solutions, love bombing, asceticism, constant activity; publications/media/home visits; planning and strategy; vision and participation; teaching and community). Very good answers explain how methods keep members.

rows.prompt: Describe the origins, beliefs and lifestyle of the Hare Krishna movement.
rows.model_answer: The Hare Krishna movement, or ISKCON, was founded in America in 1968 but has Indian roots. Its founder, Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, a successful Indian pharmacist, wrote about his ideas in the magazine 'Back to the Godhead' from 1944. At fifty-eight he left his wife and five children to become a Hindu monk, and in 1965 he went to America, where his Western-style Hindu philosophy aroused huge interest. He is honoured as God's 'via media'. The main scripture is the Bhagavad Gita, part of the Mahabharata, which tells of Krishna, the eighth incarnation of Vishnu. Members believe Krishna is the highest god and the Absolute Truth; salvation is a personal relationship with Krishna, awakened by chanting the Hare Krishna mantra. Jesus was a pure devotee of Krishna, and the soul is reincarnated according to how one lives. There are nine daily acts of devotional service, such as chanting Krishna's names and preparing food as an offering. Followers have shaven heads and saffron robes, are strict vegetarians, avoid tea, coffee, alcohol, smoking and gambling, and live in temples under a leader who arranges marriages. Their day begins at 3.00 a.m. with chanting, followed by study, chores and fundraising on the streets.

Origins (Prabhupada, pharmacist, 1944 magazine, monk at 58, America 1965, ISKCON 1968, via media); beliefs (Bhagavad Gita, Krishna eighth incarnation of Vishnu, mantra, salvation as relationship, Jesus, reincarnation, nine acts); lifestyle (robes, diet, rules, temples, leader, daily routine, initiation by fire). All three parts needed for top band.

rows.prompt: 'New Age is not a religion, but is nonetheless religious.' Discuss this statement with reference to the beliefs and practices of the New Age movement.
rows.model_answer: The New Age movement is hard to define. It is an umbrella term covering Eastern traditions, holistic health, magic, astrology and ecology, and Philip Barnes notes it has no single founder and no official creed. It is best seen as a network of groups and individuals with overlapping goals, inspired by figures such as Shirley MacLaine, Fritjof Capra, Sir George Trevelyan, Matthew Fox, Helena Blavatsky and Alice Bailey. So it is not a religion in the usual sense. Yet it is religious: its central belief is that a new age of peace and enlightenment, the Age of Aquarius, has replaced the failed Age of Pisces, and that people must create their own salvation and develop mystical awareness. It uses religious language in new ways: Christ is 'the collective conscience of the universe', a 'Cosmic Christ' is awaited, and Lucifer is the source of wisdom. It tends to divinise humanity, as in MacLaine's 'I am God'. Practices include horoscopes, yoga, tarot, channelling, crystals and chanting. Cardinal Danneels identifies four cornerstones: a scientific base, Oriental religions, a new psychology and astrology. He offers a Christian response stressing prayer and the 'I-Thou' relationship with God. Today the promised world fraternity is not materialising and the movement seems in decline.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: umbrella term; no founder or creed; network; spokespersons; Age of Aquarius vs Pisces; self-salvation; redefined terms (Cosmic Christ, Lucifer); divinising humanity; practices; common emphases; Danneels' four cornerstones and Christian response; decline. Must address both 'not a religion' and 'religious'.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between a cult and a sect, giving examples of each.
rows.model_answer: A sect is a religious group that separates from its parent religion but keeps the same world view and acknowledges the same sources of revelation. It emphasises particular aspects of the parent religion. All major world religions have developed sects over time. In Judaism, Hasidic Jews are ultra-orthodox in belief and practice. In Christianity, Methodism began as a revivalist movement within the Anglican Church. In Buddhism, Soka Gakkai and Zen Buddhism are sects. A cult, on the other hand, is any religious group that differs significantly, in one or more respects of belief or practice, from the religious groups regarded as the normal or standard expressions of religion in the culture. Examples are the Branch Davidian Movement led by David Koresh, the Children of God Movement led by David Beg and the Unification Church (Moonies) under Sun Myung Moon. The words are often used interchangeably, and people wrongly assume all cults are bad.
rows.marking_scheme: Definition of sect 2 marks + example 1 mark; definition of cult 2 marks + example 1 mark; clear statement of the difference 4 marks (sect keeps parent world view and sources of revelation; cult differs significantly from normative religion).
